messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Vulnerability: Being naked, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Exercise: Exercise
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh is a 46-year-old Vietnamese American software engineer who came to the clinic after his wife issued what she described, quietly and with evident exhaustion, as a final appeal. His PCL-5 score of 72 places him in the severe range, and within the first two sessions it became clear that the presentation had been consolidating, largely unseen, for years.

Minh served in a multinational peacekeeping capacity in his early twenties, attached to a unit that came under sustained ambush in a forested corridor. What he remembers — and cannot stop remembering — centres on the moment a motorcycle-mounted combatant accelerated through a checkpoint, the engine sound rising before anyone could respond, and the smell of burning fuel and scorched clothing that followed the explosion. He was unhurt in any way that showed on a body, but the man beside him was not. Minh has never been able to narrate what happened next in words; when he tries, language simply fails him, and he sits with his hands open on his knees as though waiting for something to arrive that does not. Instead, the event returns as a looping visual sequence — a film, he says, that no one asked him to watch — accompanied by the auditory residue of that engine climbing in pitch, replaying with a fidelity that makes the original and the present moment briefly indistinguishable.

The triggers that activate this memory are precise and merciless. The sound of a motorcycle accelerating — commonplace in any American suburb, inescapable in the parking structure near his office — pulls the film into motion immediately. Certain smells, particularly anything that carries the quality of burnt fuel or synthetic fabric, do the same. And in a way that took longer to understand, physical vulnerability has become its own trigger: being undressed, even alone in his own bathroom, carries an exposure he cannot tolerate. Each of these triggers, once encountered, floods him with the sensory and emotional texture of the ambush, and the intrusive memories themselves — looping, wordless, acoustically vivid — sustain and amplify a pervasive sense of threat that extends far beyond any rational assessment of his current environment.

Minh has come to believe, with the quiet certainty of a man who has tested his theory many times, that the world outside his routines is genuinely dangerous. He feels on guard even at home, scanning rooms before settling, sitting with his back to walls. Strangers who approach him in ordinary situations — a colleague stopping by his desk, a neighbour crossing the street toward him — register as threats before any conscious evaluation occurs. Unfamiliar places are avoided entirely because he cannot pre-map the exits or assess who might be there. This sustained threat appraisal does not merely accompany the triggers; it actively generates them, because a nervous system primed for danger finds the motorcycle noise and the unfamiliar smell before a more settled mind would register either.

Over months and then years, Minh constructed a life shaped by what he was trying not to encounter. He stopped watching television — too many films carry combat sequences, too many news programmes carry the sounds and smells of violence. He stopped going out socially, then stopped going out except for work and essential errands. He stopped exercising, because the gym is full of strangers and unpredictable sounds, and because physical exertion produces a bodily arousal state he has learned to associate with danger. These strategies succeeded, partially, in reducing the frequency of triggers — but the narrowing of his world meant that the memories were never tested against ordinary experience, never allowed to become past rather than present. Avoidance preserved the intrusive material intact. And because he no longer moved through the world with any ease, the threat appraisal remained unchallenged: every unfamiliar place he did not enter confirmed that unfamiliar places were not safe. The maintenance cycle sealed itself quietly, in the absence of incident.

His wife has watched him grow smaller inside their house. He works remotely now, which removed the parking structure problem but created a new one: he rarely leaves at all. What brought him to the clinic was not a crisis but an accumulation — her face one evening, and the recognition that he could not explain to her, or to himself, why he was still, at 46, listening for a motorcycle that had already passed.
